\(1 \pm \sqrt{2}\)
Let \(y=2-x\), so \(x+y=2\) and \(x^{4}+y^{4}=34\). We know

\[(x+y)^{4}=x^{4}+4 x^{3} y+6 x^{2} y^{2}+4 x y^{3}+y^{4}=x^{4}+y^{4}+2 x y\left(2 x^{2}+2 y^{2}+3 x y\right)\]

Moreover, \(x^{2}+y^{2}=(x+y)^{2}-2 x y\), so the preceding equation becomes \(2^{4}=34+2 x y(2\). \(2^{2}-x y\) ), or \((x y)^{2}-8 x y-9=0\). Hence \(x y=9\) or -1 . Solving \(x y=9, x+y=2\) produces complex solutions, and solving \(x y=-1, x+y=2\) produces \((x, y)=(1+\sqrt{2}, 1-\sqrt{2})\) or \((1-\sqrt{2}, 1+\sqrt{2})\). Thus, \(x=1 \pm \sqrt{2}\).
